items.title: Navigating legal liabilities: Understanding DPDP execution
items.summary: In this ‘Leading Questions’ section, Sidhant Dhingra and Shikher Upadhyay explain DPDP execution by outlining Data Fiduciary responsibilities, Significant Data Fiduciary duties, strict protections for children’s data, and rules for data erasure and retention. Question: What constitutes "Reasonable Security Safeguards" under Section 8(5), DPDP Act and Rule 6, DPDP Rules? Answer: Rule 6 sets baseline legal requirements for Section 8(5) compliance. At a minimum, Data Fiduciaries must implement: Technical safeguards, including encryption, obfuscation, masking, or tokenisation. Access control mechanisms and continuous system monitoring. Mandatory log retention for at least one year for breach detection and investigation. Business continuity plans to ensure processing stability during security incidents. Binding contractual clauses requiring Data Processors to adopt equivalent safeguards. Because "reasonableness" is evaluated retrospectively during regulatory inquiries, maintaining detailed security documentation is essential. items.title: Supreme Court says UP Gangsters Act ‘stillborn’, quashes cases against two lawyers
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday held that the Uttar Pradesh Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986 is “stillborn” since it prescribes punishment without creating a distinct criminal offence [Shiv Pratap Singh alias Chinu v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Others]. A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said the Act merely defines a 'gang' and a 'gangster' while activities covered by these definitions are already punishable under the IPC and other penal laws. “ After defining gang, which includes commission of the offences listed under sub-clauses (i) to (xxv) and defining gangster as a member or leader or organiser of a gang, the punishment is prescribed for a gangster without an offence being created by statute; which makes the penal act, stillborn ,” the Court said in its judgment. The Court invoked George Orwell to say that the legislation was perpetuating violence against unsuspecting citizens while purporting to prevent it. In an order passed on August 19, Justice Ghosh said the incident took place on August 18, a day after she had reserved her judgment on Bose’s bail plea. According to the judge, while she was in the courtroom, one of the lawyers appearing for Bose, along with judge's private secretary, went to the judge's chamber and asked her staff to bring out the records of the case. Justice M Nagaprasanna modified Nagendra's bail terms to permit him to travel outside Karnataka and anywhere within India. However, the Minster continues to be restrained from travelling out of the country unless he gets permission from the Court to do so. The Court passed the order after nothing that since Nagendra holds a cabinet position, he should be permitted to travel outside the State of Karnataka and within India. "The petitioner being a cabinet minister is admitted fact. In light of the ministerial position, and holding A portfolio or B portfolio would necessitate travel beyond jurisidction. The petitioner is free to travel within the country as not permitting travel would undoubtedly curtail his liberty and the position that he is holding today," the Court said. items.title: Illegal, irrational: Delhi HC criticises ED for adding 6-year-old FIR to ECIR to keep PMLA case alive
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has come down heavily on the Enforcement Directorate (ED) for the manner in which it tried to sustain a money laundering case after the First Information Report (FIR) forming the basis of its Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR) was closed by a court [Kanchana Rai v Directorate of Enforcement + connected matters]. ED was investigating money laundering allegations against certain family members of late Rajya Sabha MP Dr. Mahendra Prasad, the founder of Aristo Pharmaceuticals, whose net worth is estimated to be over ₹4,000 crores. His family is now engaged in a bitter dispute over the control of his assets. In a judgment delivered on August 18, Justice Anish Dayal noted that the ED had added a 2019 FIR to the ECIR through an addendum in August 2025, despite being aware of its existence since at least 2023. The addendum was issued only after a Delhi magistrate court accepted the Economic Offences Wing’s (EOW) cancellation report in June 2025 and closed the 2021 FIR on which the ED’s case was originally based. Sanjush was allegedly driving an Aston Martin at a high speed when the car hit Bharati Mukhi, a sales associate at a Lifestyle store in the Inorbit Mall in Madhapur, Hyderabad. Bharati was crossing the road while bringing lunch from a place nearby and returning to work, according to the complaint filed by the store manager Aswin Kumar. Madhapur ACP Ch Sridhar said Sanjush was not arrested because the offence registered against him is bailable and carries a maximum punishment of less than seven years. Police only served him a notice, he said. Sanjush was booked under Section 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita – causing death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide – which carries a maximum punishment of five years’ imprisonment and a fine. “As the punishment is below seven years, it is bailable. items.title: MAP Bengaluru’s ‘Grip, Hold, Pin’ traces Indian wrestling through art and photography
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Wrestling in India has long existed beyond the ring, in mythology, sculpture, photographs and the akharas , where generations of wrestlers have trained. But the sport has also been shaped by questions of caste, gender, power and survival. At Bengaluru's Museum of Art and Photography (MAP), a new exhibition brings these different histories together. Grip, Hold, Pin , which opened on August 15, traces Indian wrestling through photographs and artworks spanning decades, from archival images by Raghu Rai, TS Satyan and Jyoti Bhatt to contemporary work by Indrajit Khambe and Prarthna Singh. Curated by Aayati Sengupta, the exhibition looks at what happens around wrestling as much as the sport itself — the bodies, spaces, rituals and communities that sustain it. It also arrives at a time when Indian wrestling is faced with renewed scrutiny over questions of power and gender. The exhibition grew out of an unexpected discovery in MAP's own collection.
